planningContext.motion: Is belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God rational given alleged gratuitous evil, salvation confusion, rationality, design, and morality?

routes.description: Establish that belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God is irrational because the available evidence includes apparently gratuitous evil and confused salvation requirements, while the proposed arguments from reason, design, and morality do not adequately support that God.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the conflict between the claimed divine attributes and the observed world, together with epistemic and salvation confusion, defeats or outweighs the cumulative positive case for rational theism.

bridges.description: Given the available reason and evidence, belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God is irrational.

Apparently gratuitous evil and related epistemic confusion outweigh the proposed arguments for God and prevent those arguments from rationally supporting the all-powerful, all-loving God under discussion.
Pervasive suffering that appears to serve no greater good is improbable under an all-powerful, all-loving God, and merely possible theodicies do not make belief in that God rational.
An all-loving God would not attach grave eternal consequences to salvation conditions that sincere people cannot reliably identify and religious communities cannot agree upon.

Evolutionary accounts of cognition and morality, together with alternative explanations of apparent design, undercut the claim that reason, fine-tuning, or moral experience rationally identifies the proposed God.

routes.description: Establish that belief in God is rational through a cumulative case from the reliability of reason, the life-permitting structure of the universe, and objective morality, while answering the evidential challenge from suffering.
routes.successCriteria: Show that rationality, design, and morality are collectively more expected or intelligible if God exists than if God does not, and that suffering does not defeat this cumulative support.

bridges.description: The cumulative available evidence makes belief in God more rational than nonbelief.

The combined evidence from rational minds, cosmic design, and objective morality makes God more probable than God's nonexistence, while available responses prevent suffering from defeating that inference.
Unguided naturalism undermines confidence that evolved minds track truth, whereas an intelligent creator provides a rational basis for trusting human reason and the universe's intelligibility.
The universe's highly specific life-permitting conditions are substantially more probable under intelligent design than under an unguided chance hypothesis.
Objective moral obligations are difficult to ground in an impersonal, purposeless universe but are intelligible when goodness is grounded in God.

sections.title: Rational Belief and the Reliability of Human Reason
sections.rationale: Beginning with the debate’s definition of rational belief, this section groups the competing accounts of why human cognition can be trusted and the ensuing exchange over evolutionary truth-tracking and theistic reliability.

moveAssignments.rationale: This definition supplies the evidential standard that organizes the later dispute over whether theistic belief is rational rather than merely true or false.
This constructive states the principal theistic inference from reliable minds and an intelligible universe to an intelligent creator.
This move develops the evolutionary reliability challenge in full and distinguishes unguided evolution from a process intended by God to produce rational knowers.
This reply supplies two major structural objections: the separation of atheism from naturalism and the distinction between undermining an alternative and establishing theism.
This move provides the central evolutionary counteraccount, linking broadly accurate representation to the survival costs of systematically false beliefs.
This reply restates the contrast between truth as an intended cognitive function and truth as an intermittent correlate of evolutionary success.
This move completes the exchange by arguing that inaccessible divine reasoning creates an analogous reliability problem for the theistic account.

sections.title: Gratuitous Evil, Theodicy, and Restoration
sections.rationale: This section collects the initial evidential challenge from apparently purposeless suffering, the evil-God comparison, the concession about its significance, and the principal theistic accounts of normativity, afterlife, theodicy, and divine participation in suffering.

moveAssignments.rationale: This constructive introduces the debate’s principal suffering-based challenge by contrasting observed apparently gratuitous evil with the asserted divine attributes.
The evil-God comparison supplies a central probability test for possible reconciliations and develops the initial suffering argument beyond simple inconsistency.
This concession marks suffering as a central point of dispute while serving mainly as a transition into the con side’s substantive replies.
This reply introduces a normative contrast between Christianity’s account of a world that ought to be otherwise and a universe characterized by indifference.
This move adds the afterlife and possible restoration to the temporal frame within which earthly suffering is assessed.
This reply gathers the principal theodicy families and the claim of divine participation in suffering into the con side’s response structure.

sections.title: Salvation Confusion and the Identity of God
sections.rationale: This section connects the critique of disputed salvation conditions with the cumulative case for rational theism and the later contention that generic creator arguments do not by themselves identify an all-powerful, all-loving religious God.

moveAssignments.rationale: This constructive states the salvation-confusion problem through the combination of grave consequences and disagreement about the beliefs required for salvation.
This move develops the salvation critique by connecting hidden or disputed requirements with divine love, human access, and threatened punishment.
This constructive integrates the arguments from rationality, design, and morality into the con side’s cumulative motion-level case.
This reply directly addresses what the cumulative arguments could identify by separating a generic creator from the all-powerful, all-loving God under debate.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning and Evolutionary Accounts of Design
sections.rationale: This section places the cosmic fine-tuning argument alongside the later evolutionary account of apparent biological design, preserving the debate’s distinct but related explanations of ordered and life-permitting features.

moveAssignments.rationale: This constructive supplies the section’s principal design inference from narrow life-permitting physical conditions to intelligent calibration.
This move provides the pro side’s natural explanatory alternative for apparent biological design and locates its significance within changing available evidence.

sections.title: Objective Morality, Evolution, and Divine Goodness
sections.rationale: This section groups the moral argument for God, the evolutionary account of moral intuitions, and the extended exchange over whether goodness is independent of God, arbitrarily commanded, or grounded in the divine nature.

moveAssignments.rationale: This constructive states the principal moral argument by presenting objective moral obligation as requiring an explanation grounded in God.
This reply supplies an evolutionary account of care, sacrifice, moral intuition, and the emotional force of religious narratives.
This move introduces the section’s central dilemma concerning whether goodness exists independently of God or depends on divine command.
This reply adds the historical claim that biblical teaching about divine image-bearing helped furnish the moral standards used in the critique.
This move states the principal divine-nature response by grounding objective goodness in God rather than in an external standard or arbitrary command.
This reply completes the exchange by arguing that identifying God with goodness restates rather than removes the underlying dilemma.

bridgeMappings.rationale: The retained evidence spans the governing rationality standard, the principal challenges from suffering and salvation confusion, and the later argument about whether a creator can be identified with the God specified by the motion.

These moves preserve the structural comparison between evil and epistemic confusion on one side and the cumulative positive case on the other, including the dispute over what kind of deity that case could establish.

The mapping retains the full suffering exchange: apparently gratuitous evil, the evil-God comparison, the concession about its centrality, normative and afterlife replies, recognized theodicies, and the later divine-identity consequence.
Both retained moves are assigned together because they state and develop the same salvation-confusion line concerning severe consequences, disputed requirements, limited access, and divine love.

The retained evidence is distributed across the three relevant explanatory disputes: cognitive reliability, apparent design, and morality. Together those sections preserve the evolutionary and alternative-explanation material associated with this bridge.
The mapping retains the three constructive strands from reason, design, and morality as well as the move that explicitly combines them into the con side’s cumulative case concerning rational belief.

These retained moves preserve every component of the cumulative structure: reason, fine-tuning, morality, their explicit combination, and the concession and replies intended to keep suffering within the same overall evidential comparison.

All retained evidence for this bridge is grouped in the rationality section, including the unguided-evolution challenge, the guided-evolution contrast, and the successive evolutionary and parity-based replies.

The mapping places the fine-tuning constructive and the evolutionary account of apparent design in the design section while retaining the later creator-identity reply in the section addressing what such arguments could establish.

The morality section retains the objective-morality constructive, evolutionary alternative, divine-command dilemma, historical biblical account, divine-nature response, and final restatement objection as one complete topical exchange.

sections.title: Rational-Belief Standard and Cumulative Case
sections.rationale: This opening section establishes the governing distinction between rationality and truth, then pairs it with the cumulative theistic conclusion that the debate subsequently tests across several evidential domains.

moveAssignments.rationale: This move supplies the debate-wide standard of rational belief against which the later constructive arguments and exchanges are organized.
This move states the cumulative theistic conclusion that integrates the later lines concerning rationality, design, and morality.

sections.title: Evil, Salvation Confusion, and Divine Character
sections.rationale: This section groups the early challenges from apparently gratuitous suffering and disputed salvation conditions with the later theistic concessions, defenses, and creator-versus-classical-God synthesis.

moveAssignments.rationale: This is a load-bearing statement of the apparent-gratuitous-evil challenge to the specified all-powerful and all-loving God.
The evil-God comparison provides a major structural test of whether possible reconciliations adequately address the suffering challenge.
This move introduces the distinct salvation-confusion burden concerning grave consequences and disagreement about necessary beliefs.
This move develops the salvation-confusion line through the disputed and inaccessible salvation-hoop formulation.
The concession identifies suffering as the principal counterevidence before the section turns to the proposed theistic responses.
This reply connects the experience of suffering to a normative account of how the world ought to be.
This reply introduces afterlife restoration as a major component of the proposed accounting for earthly suffering.
This move consolidates the section's named theodicies and the claim that God participates in and responds to suffering.
This synthesis connects the suffering dispute to whether any inferred creator can be identified with the specified classical God.

sections.title: Evolution and the Reliability of Reason
sections.rationale: This section contains the evolutionary reliability case for theism and the ensuing exchange over naturalism, truth-tracking, adaptive cognition, and whether theism faces an analogous reliability problem.

moveAssignments.rationale: This move states the principal constructive contrast between unguided minds and reason grounded in an intelligent creator.
This move supplies the detailed evolutionary argument that natural selection targets advantageous behavior rather than truth.
This reply separates atheism from naturalism and raises the adaptive-cost challenge to systematically false cognition.
This move develops the evolutionary account of broadly accurate but imperfect cognition as a major opposing step.
This reply restates the theistic truth-directed account and contrasts it with cognition directed toward evolutionary success.
This move closes the exchange by arguing that inaccessible divine reasoning creates an analogous trust problem for theism.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning and Natural Accounts of Design
sections.rationale: This section pairs the fine-tuning argument from narrow life-permitting physical conditions with the later evolutionary account offered as an alternative explanation for apparent biological design.

moveAssignments.rationale: This move is the section's load-bearing constructive statement of fine-tuning as evidence for intelligent design.
This move supplies the section's principal naturalistic alternative by locating apparent biological design within evolutionary explanation.

sections.title: Objective Morality and the Ground of Goodness
sections.rationale: This section follows the moral argument from objective obligations through evolutionary explanation, the divine-command dilemma, the historical biblical reply, divine-nature grounding, and the final restatement.

moveAssignments.rationale: This move states the load-bearing moral argument that objective moral law requires grounding and is explained by God.
This reply offers social evolution as an alternative account of moral intuitions, care, sacrifice, and religious resonance.
This move introduces the central dilemma between morality independent of God and morality defined by divine command.
This reply connects the moral standards used in criticism to the historical influence of biblical human dignity.
This move gives the principal divine-nature response by grounding objective goodness in God as the personal creator.
This closing reply argues that identifying God with goodness restates rather than removes the underlying dilemma.

bridgeMappings.rationale: The retained evidence spans the opening rational-belief standard and the later evil, salvation, and divine-identity material that carries the motion-level pro route.
The mapping preserves the cumulative-case reference in the opening frame and the concentrated evidence concerning evil, epistemic confusion, salvation, and identification of the proposed God.

All retained evidence for the suffering subsidiary is concentrated in the section containing apparent gratuitous evil, the evil-God comparison, concessions, theodicies, restoration, and divine identity.

The two retained salvation-confusion moves are assigned together because they state the disagreement over salvation requirements and develop the inaccessible-hoop consequence within one topical section.
The retained evidence is distributed across the three relevant domains: evolved cognition and reason, natural explanations of apparent design, and evolutionary or independent accounts of morality.
The cumulative conclusion is retained in the opening frame, while its three constructive evidential components remain assigned to the reason, design, and morality sections.
This mapping retains the cumulative conclusion, each positive evidential line, and the responses to suffering across their topical sections, preserving the complete central route structure.
All retained evidence concerning evolved minds, truth-tracking, intelligent creation, and the reciprocal reliability challenge is assigned to the dedicated reason section.

The fine-tuning constructive and natural-design alternative are grouped in the design section, while the later creator-identification synthesis remains in the divine-character section where it occurs topically.

The complete retained morality exchange is assigned to one section, covering objective moral law, evolutionary explanation, the divine-command dilemma, biblical influence, and divine-nature grounding.
